To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Swedish manufacturing industries experienced a mushroom-like growth pattern and that steam power was not a general purpose technology in Sweden.
the growth of total factor productivity (TFP) was uneven, mushroom-like, and that electricity, not steam, may have contributed to this pattern in the last decade of the nineteenth century.

(a) Swedish manufacturing industries experienced a mushroom-like pattern of productivity growth in the four decades preceding the First World World War, and (b) this pattern of productivity growth is consistent with the idea that steam power was not a general purpose technology in the sense that it did not affect productivity growth across industries in a systematic way, and that the use of electricity was not a necessary condition for a yeast-like pattern of productivity to emerge.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether or not there was a general purpose steam technology in Swedish manufacturing.
the question of whether or not the Swedish economy experienced a Harberger's yeast pattern of productivity growth during the period of the Industrial Revolution.
the role of general purpose technologies in the growth process of the Swedish manufacturing industries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence does not allow for a definite verdict on the issue of whether the growth process in Swedish manufacturing was yeast or mushroom like.
steam was not the general purpose technology in Sweden, but electricity may have been.
the evidence does not support a yeast-like pattern, and that the evidence is too weak to support a mushroom-like pattern.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evidence does not support the idea that a general purpose technology was in operation during the period under study.
the evidence does not support the idea that the steam engine was a general purpose machine.

the Swedish economy was characterized by a mushroom pattern of productivity growth across industries, and that the mushroom-like progress in the 1890s and 1900s was not caused by a single general purpose technology, but by a number of technologies that spilled over to a small number of manufacturing processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the yeast versus mushrooms dichotomization is a powerful tool in analyzing the growth of productivity across industries.
, in the case of Swedish manufacturing industries, the mushroom pattern of productivity growth is the more likely one.
, in the absence of a general purpose technology, the mushroom pattern is more common than the yeast pattern.
